segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back in the '60s, when Stephen was a young surgeon in Boston, a guy came in with abdominal pain, which turned out to be his gallbladder. He needed an operation. But the guy told Stephen this story of how, 12 years before, he'd come into that exact same hospital and had had cancer. It started in his stomach and had spread to his belly. The doctors opened him up.

segments.speaker: Dr. Stephen Rosenberg
segments.text: And the surgeons had seen cancer that had spread into his liver and throughout his abdomen. They could do nothing and they just closed the abdomen and sent him home to die. And yet, here he was 12 years later, seeming quite healthy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Stephen was skeptical. Cancer usually does not just go away with no treatment at all. The guy must have gotten the story wrong in some way.

segments.speaker: Dr. Stephen Rosenberg
segments.text: Then I went back to the patient's chart and I read, in fact, the pathology reports. And I was still skeptical. So then I went back and actually pulled out the slides to be sure in fact he had had the cancer. And we reviewed the slides, and in fact, it was a cancer. And then I made sure it was in fact the same patient. And in fact, it was.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then when you opened him up, were you fully expecting you were going to still find some cancer?

segments.speaker: Dr. Stephen Rosenberg
segments.text: Well, it was 12 years later and I didn't know what to expect. I operated on him, took out his gallbladder, examined the inside of his abdomen, and all of the cancer that had been present 12 years earlier had completely disappeared in the absence of any treatment.

segments.speaker: Dr. Stephen Rosenberg
segments.text: It appeared that this patient's body had somehow rejected his cancer. This patient set me on a quest for the next 25 years to try to explain how such a thing could happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in fact, this doctor, Stephen Rosenberg, is now a pioneer in inventing immunotherapies based on that research at The National Cancer Institute, where he's chief of surgery. Now, it's interesting, you can find the story about this early case of his all over the place. It circulates on the internet, it shows up in books about people spontaneously recovering from cancer, and he is not happy about that. He kind of hates it, in fact. Because he says that this story gives people false hope. In his career, he's seen maybe 10,000 cancer patients, and this is the only case like this that he has ever encountered. It is just fantastically rare. And it is so easy, he says, for patients to get their hopes up. How could anybody not get their hopes up? And Dr. Rosenberg has seen lots of patients taken advantage of by people who play on this dream of a spontaneous recovery.

segments.speaker: Dr. Stephen Rosenberg
segments.text: People who prey on cancer patients, offering quack treatments, often take advantage of cancer patients who are desperate. And I've seen entire families devastated as their entire resources are devoted to treatments of no value.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Still, hope is important. So what do you do when people place hope in things that probably are not going to work? Well, lots of times his patients come to him asking about vitamins, and herbs, and visualization, and other treatments that have not been proven by science. And if the treatments aren't actually going to hurt them in any way, he says, sure, do it. Studies have shown that patients who are embracing life, feeling more hopeful, feeling more in control of their situation, do better, respond better to medical treatment of all kinds. There are real health effects to hope itself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so, today on our radio show, we have two stories of hope, the power of hope, hope in some things that are not very likely, I have to say. We have stories about the great side of that and the maybe less great side of that. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life , distributed by Public Radio International. I'm Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our program today in two acts. Act One, a son tries to help his mom in a faraway place defy the laws of medical science. Act Two, a daughter tries to help her dad by going to a faraway place to defy the laws of the United States of America. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: This is the problem. My mom's trying to use my belief in channeling to get me to belief in Joao.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, just to remind people of how you've talked about this in the past, your mom channels this ancient being, Aaron. And the last time you came on the show and talked about it, you described it this way. You said that, basically you faced this choice as her kid. You could decide that channeling isn't real and your mom's a little crazy. And you don't think she's crazy. She's really wonderful in so many ways. And so you sort of provisionally were thinking, OK, well, maybe this is real.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Yeah. And I've seen the work that she does with Aaron. And I've seen how helpful it is to people.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Aaron gives people advice?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Yeah, so I've seen the good that comes out of that. But now she's upping the stakes. She's saying, if I'm going to keep believing in Aaron and that stuff, I also have to believe in Joao and the entities.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it's like you're at a kind of showdown with her?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Yeah. And I didn't realize this was going to happen. But it's true, at home it's easy to sort of each believe what we want to believe and just, it never has to come to a head.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So is there any point down there when you thought that you started to believe a little bit?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Yeah, actually. There was one day.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: All those who have surgery, please raise there hand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what's going on now?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: We're at the Casa. We're going to see some physical surgeries.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, you mean like real surgeries?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Yeah, knife.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He does those, too?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Yeah. He cuts into people. Scrapes their eyes. No anesthetic. Joao wouldn't let me record the operations, but he let me stand right there next to him while he did them.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: I knew this morning that a couple of the people I'd gotten to be friends with, Gregor and Cynthia, they're from Baltimore. Gregor has MS, so he's in a wheelchair. And Cynthia has some ailments, so she wanted to get surgery, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so how's it go? You go in there with Cynthia and she's in there with him. What's he do?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Well, she's standing there with her eyes closed and he just kind of tilts her head back a little bit. He's got this wicked-looking instrument. They call it a Kelly clamp. It's about seven inches long. It's basically a long, metal skinny scissors with a little cotton ball kind of in the pliers tip of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, I can feel where this is going. Let me just warn people, this might get a little graphic. OK, continue Davy.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: He tilts her head back. He dips the point of it just kind of up her right nostril. And then he turns around and just slams it all the way in, so just all the way to the handle, straight back into her head.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh my God.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: It was horrifying. It was the most upsetting thing I've ever seen. The room kind of started swirling around me. And everything got really silent. There's sort of like a roar fills your ears. And I just kept watching as he started kind of poking and jabbing around in there. It was like if you're trying to scrape in a jar of peanut butter to get the last little bit out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, and so what is she doing? Is she like screaming? Like, what's she doing?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: She's just standing there, pretty calmly. I mean, she looks maybe a little uncomfortable. But she's very calm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then what happens?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Well, then after 30 seconds of that, he pulls the thing out and she kind of just collapses into a chair. And they wheel her off into this sort of infirmary. And that's the last I see of her for a little while. So I go and just sit down in one of these chairs for another hour or two. I'm freaking out. Because like, I just saw something that should not be possible, that there's no way that could happen. What he just did should have killed her and it didn't. I have to say, it was an hour or two like I've never had before. And I was just completely shaken. I was just sitting there and I didn't know what to believe.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: After I'd been sitting there for a couple hours, I went outside and I was standing with Gregor, her husband, who's in a wheelchair. And he was anxious about how she was and then she comes kind of skipping out, just happy as can be. Of course, she'd had her eyes closed the whole time.

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: What does the thing actually even look like, the apparatus? Is it big or is it small? I have no idea.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: It's about a seven-inch scissors, like--

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: Scissors? Now I'm getting scared.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: I don't know if it's a good thing for me to describe it to you. Honestly, he twisted it back, so it was going like almost straight back into your brain. And then he just jammed it all the way in. I mean, I thought he had killed you. I honestly did.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so did you go and tell your mom? Like, what did your mom make of it?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: She had an explanation for exactly what was happening.

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: The frequency of vibration of these tools is raised so high that they simply become energy and light. Material is transmuted literally into light. And then, as the instrument withdraws the tool, he releases that energy thrust into it and it turns back into the metal that it was.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Then I had talked to a couple doctors and it turns out there's a cavity behind the nose and it goes back a long way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, so there's room for the instrument?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Right. And your brain's surround by bone, so there's no way you can harm it or help it, for that matter, by sticking something up your nose. So really, what Joao did, in the end, isn't proof of miracles, but proof of sinus cavities.

segments.speaker: Alexander
segments.text: Some day I'm not good, some day I'm very good. It's with ups and downs. That's it.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: There's this couple, Tatiana and Ed. They were from Holland. And you saw them all the time pushing their son around the Casa in a wheelchair, Alexander. He had muscular dystrophy. And the doctors in Holland had said there was no cure, like nothing that could be done for him. Here's Tatiana.

segments.speaker: Tatiana
segments.text: You know what? The worst in this illness is that you feel helpless. You feel so very helpless. You know that this boy will die little by little every day in front of your eyes, and you can't do anything. It makes you furious. From time to time, you're furious. You're saying, why? Well, I want to do something about that. I can't just watch it happening like that. This is the only, our chance, and the last one.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Tatiana hadn't believed in any of this stuff before Alexander got sick. But her and Ed were willing to try anything. The doctors had told them that the muscles would just deteriorate until, at age 18 or so, your heart just can no longer even beat, and he'd die. This is Alexander. He's 10.

segments.speaker: Alexander
segments.text: Well, the entities, they told us positive concentration. So we're working on that. We're doing our best.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: What's that?

segments.speaker: Alexander
segments.text: We're doing our best.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Have they told you that you will be healed?

segments.speaker: Alexander
segments.text: Yes, they said a couple of times, he will walk. And then he said another time, you will walk very soon. What soon is for the entities, we don't know.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: To me, when I meet people like this, hoping for a miracle, it's really the only choice you have. It seems completely sane to me. It's the logical choice.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: One night, one of the posadas hired an accordion player and had a little dance. And everyone was there. Maggie, she's blind, and she's dancing with Dennis. Gregor, who uses a walker at home, but he gets up and twirls for a second with Cynthia. Then he topples over again. I mean, everyone who's here, they are so joyful just being together and having hope. And whether or not you believe in the spirits and everything, it just seems like it's good for you. It improves your health to be in a beautiful place.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: There was 25 people in my mom's group. No one was cured, but everyone was glad that they'd been there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Everybody, that is, but you?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Right. It wasn't quite enough for me. I mean, my mom still's deaf, my skin's still messed up, and Joao told both of us we needed to come back for more visits. And the worst thing was, my mom and I, we were not seeing eye to eye.

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: The thing is, can you open your heart to the possibility that this is real, and that in three or four years you could be healed if you do what you need to do? Do you know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Kind of, but I just think you and I see the world differently.

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: We probably do. We're two different people. I used to see the world the way you do and I've learned some things by banging my head against the wall and then stopping because I realized it wasn't getting me anywhere.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: I'm not banging my head. I don't think there is a master plan. I don't think there is a reason for everything. I think there are accidents and coincidences.

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: I don't. And I'm not going to argue that one with you. I don't know, Davy. I would hope that you can just say, let's see what happens.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: I don't want to let you down, but I don't think I'm going to come back here unless it's to visit you because you've moved here or something.

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: You don't think you would come back even though he says he can cure you? That's up to you. That's entirely up to you. That's hard for me to understand why.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: I don't really believe in it.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: That was the first time I had ever told her that, and maybe realized it myself. I don't know what that means exactly for me and my mom.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You mean, for the two of you who are so close to say, we disagree on something that's so fundamental and such a big part of her life?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Right, because it is everything to her. It's been a couple months since we got back, and she says that she's experiencing some changes. And other people from the group, Maggie, who was blind is saying she's beginning to see a little bit. For my mom, it's the same thing. She says she can feel her inner ears. She can feel changes, shifts, vibrations, and she thinks it's the beginning of hearing.

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: I can feel my voice going up and down. Suddenly, I have some sense of where the notes are. It's completely different.

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: Do you hear the difference?

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: It's like hearing. It's just vibration. I'm hearing it. I've got to get the tunes, the notes. [SINGING] Amazing grace, how sweet the sound, that saved a soul like me. [END SINGING]

segments.speaker: Barbara
segments.text: Am I way off? Am I better than I was before?

segments.speaker: Davy Rothbart
segments.text: It sounded beautiful to me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Davy Rothbart is about to head out on a 126-city tour for his new book of excerpts from Found magazine, the magazine he created. Details are at foundmagazine.com.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC -  "AMAZING GRACE" BY DESTINY'S CHILD FEATURING MISSY ELLIOT]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, summoning the mysterious entities known as the Food and Drug Administration. That's in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life , I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose some theme, bring you a variety of different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's program, Miracle Cures. Stories of kids doing whatever they think it might take, doing the impossible to help their parents get cured. We've arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two is this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Julia Whitty's dad had cancer, and he had used up all the available kinds of treatment. He probably just had a few months left to live. But there was one hope for him, one last drug that might work. And the problem was, a year of this drug would cost him $47,000, which his insurance couldn't cover and which he could not afford.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Julia Whitty, she just wrote a magazine article about this experience. She said that she found when she tried to find this drug for him, she found that most of the ways she could get the drug for less were not exactly legal.

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: I absolutely was willing to break the law and I can't imagine too many people who wouldn't be, in all honesty. If you clearly saw there was a source for what you needed, and if you had to break the law a little bit to cross over the line to go there and get it, I think most people would do that for somebody that they loved. So that was where I began to look around and see if there was some other way we could get this drug.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you started looking around, what'd you find?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: I went on the internet, as most people would in this day and age, I just started surfing around. And I did find-- that's where I first came in contact with people who might have had a loved one who died and had leftover prescription that they would sometimes give away or sell. But obviously, we needed a steady, reliable, long-term dose of this stuff. And I eventually was able to locate a country that manufactured this drug for completely different diseases. And they were selling it for about $1,200 a year, which obviously started to sound really cheap.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As compared with $47,000 per year?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you go, you fly to some foreign country, you get some doctor there, I guess, to prescribe the drug?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Right, which is not difficult to do in other countries. It's pretty much not difficult to do in any country if you're a traveler.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did you have to actually claim that you had a disease or did you just tell the doctor, here's my situation.

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: I told him the truth regarding my father. And he was more than willing. I think he felt good being able to help me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And at this point, you're not exactly sure if it's legal to bring these back?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: That's right.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what do you do?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Well, I had thought about it in advance, because I travel in my adult life and I've spent a lot of time in third world countries and stuff. And I usually travel with a pretty hefty medical arsenal. You know, I'd put multiple pills in one bottle. So I thought, well, I'm just going to go there. However they come, I'm going to take them out of that packaging and put them in empty prescription bottles that I have with other prescription names on them. And in all my years of traveling, I've never come back into the US and had anybody open my bottles. So I really didn't think I was going to have trouble with this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so this is like, dozens of pills or hundreds of pills?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: It was somewhere between two-, three-, or four-month supply, enough to sort of start my father on it, do a set of scans and see whether or not it was working.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you have hundreds of pills, what was the moment like when you finally were coming back into the country?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Well, you definitely get that sweaty palms thing going. You wonder, what are they looking for? What expression on your face? You know you're doing something that could be wrong.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And what do we know about how many people are actually going overseas and bringing back drugs?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: I know that their estimates right now are that between one and two million Americans are getting drugs one way or another from Canada alone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And is that legal or is that illegal?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: In my personal experience, it was probably always illegal, but it wasn't enforced. For whatever reason, it began to be enforced around December of 2002. And I was told by the FDA that they were cracking down at that point.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you know what the penalty would have been if you'd been caught?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: I don't know, but I remember being so angry at the time that I was perfectly prepared to go to jail. Not that I want to go to jail, but I was just feeling this was an absurd way to have to live. And it was ridiculous, in light of the fact that this drug could be had more inexpensively and why my father couldn't have access to it. I considered it immoral.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, at some point you learned that you might be able to simply order the drug from, what was it, an online manufacturer? Like an online pharmacy?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Not an online pharmacy. That would have been easy. It was the actual manufacturer in this country overseas. And they claimed they were already doing it for other patients in the United States. And they told me it would just sail through US customs and that did not turn out to be the case. It gets held up in US customs in Cincinnati and I began a long series of conversations with FDA officials, sort of case officers. And they tell me, it's illegal. You can't bring this in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the reason for that law is because they can't vouch for the quality of the drugs? They haven't tested those drugs?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Exactly right. They haven't tested those drugs. That's what they say. We haven't tested those drugs, we don't know if they'll be good for you or not.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But in a way, that's a legitimate thing. Like. In a way, you'd want the government to actually do that, to say, we have no idea if this manufacturer's reputable and the drug's OK.

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Well, I would argue that I have the right to take that chance myself. We're just simply not allowed to do this. Now, we can bring in foreign-made food and foreign-made clothes and everything else, but we're not allowed to bring in foreign-made drugs because they are untested supposedly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a passage in your article where you say, "I can go to Europe and buy their wine for less, go to Asia and buy their clothes for less. American companies can buy their raw materials for less overseas, or they can move their operations abroad in order to hire cheaper labor or management. But on a mind-boggling reversal of the American principle of supply and demand, I cannot purchase cheaper drugs and bring them home."

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: That's right. And that's the part that, to this day, infuriates me, particularly about the new Medicare drug bill, which has expressly now, completely, clearly forbidden Americans to go overseas and bring back drugs for any reason whatsoever.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so the FDA holds this stuff up. How long do they hold it?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: They held it for a couple of weeks. And for the first time, we'd cut his dose in half to try and eke it out, as the package wasn't delivered. Then we cut his dose in half again. Eventually it became clear to me that they were not going to give it to us for any reason whatsoever. And in fact, they were going to destroy it. And that's when I turned to my elected officials. I thought, well, maybe they can help me on this end. One senator, Barbara Boxer, was phenomenally helpful. Her office went to work on it. They just dug their teeth in and they had that package sprung in about 24 hours.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And did you end up having to get the senator's office to intervene for you again?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Yes, I did.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like, every time it would come to the border, the same place, same people?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: No, eventually I figured out a method with the FDA guy that they were willing to accept. We had to provide these very elaborate excuses of why my father was using the foreign version versus the American version of this drug. We had to sort of basically manufacture excuses.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, I see. You had to say that the American version didn't work?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Didn't work as well for my father for the following reasons, which we pretty much made up. It was pretty bogus, but they went for it. And they did that a few times. That system worked, and then it stopped working.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why, what happened?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: At the end of 2002, we were bringing in another shipment and playing the game the way we'd learned to play it. And this time just couldn't get it sprung. And that was when I heard that the law, not that the law had changed, but that enforcement of the law had changed. And they were beginning to really crack down now on letting these drugs in.

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: The FDA case officer suggested that I go to the US company that manufactured the drug and apply for patient financial assistance.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, that's a special program which lets you say, we don't have the money to pay the $47,000, so give us a break, basically, on humanitarian grounds?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: That's right. And apparently, a lot of the pharmaceutical companies have these things, whether people know it or not, for their more expensive drugs. And we had actually applied for this at the very beginning, when my father was first prescribed this drug, and he didn't pass. He wasn't poor enough, they thought, so I decided we'd just lie. And I called the patient financial assistance line. They had an 800 number. And I was trying to sort of suss them out on, like, how poor did you really have to be before they would accept you? And she said, well, I can't tell you that. But she did, I think inadvertently, admit the only thing I really needed to know, which was that they don't actually check anything you say on the application.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, she said that to you straight out?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: She told me straight out. I felt like it was something, she went, oh God, I shouldn't have said that. And in my brain, a little bell just went off and I went, yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, a few months after your dad died-- and we should say that he didn't die of the cancer, he ended up dying of heart failure-- Congress passed the Medicare drug bill, which was designed to address exactly this problem. If your dad had survived, what would this bill have done for him, which is supposed to, basically, take these expensive drugs and put them within financial reach of people?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Well, I ran the numbers on it and I found that he would have still had to pay over $6,000 a year. And obviously, that's a lot cheaper. It's still not as cheap as the $1,200-a-year version you could get overseas.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So is that good or bad, as far as you're concerned, getting it down to $6,000 to--

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: It's not good enough. It's not good enough, in my opinion, not if the drug companies are going to be able to ask $47,000, in my father's case, for a drug that all the research and development was done more than 40 years ago. If they have the right to do that, then I think we need to have something. If the government's going to become the biggest drug buyer on the planet, then they need to do something about enacting price controls or setting standards that they're willing to pay.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The thing you're talking about is actually that, under the bill, the United States government would not be able to negotiate for lower prices. They wouldn't be able to say, we're buying a huge quantity, so give us a price break?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: Right. Congress expressly forbade that in the Medicare drug bill.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And as you note in your article, when the government buys anything in quantity, they negotiate the price down.

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: That's right. That's another case, I think, where the pharmaceutical industry wrote the law.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And do you blame the drug companies for that?

segments.speaker: Julia Whitty
segments.text: I blame the drug companies at getting through to our elected officials, yes. They're obviously phenomenally powerful, as we can see by the number of lobbyists that they employ: 600, more than one for every member of Congress. There's a personal lobbyist, in effect, for every member of Congress.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Julia Whitty's story about getting her dad's $47,000 prescription filled is in the issue of Mother Jones . That is on newsstands now, and it's at motherjones.com.
